items.title: 22/7 is a very good approximation of pi for a reason
items.claim: The fraction 22/7 = 3.142857 is closer to pi than its small denominator suggests. The fractions 355/113 = 3.141593 are even closer — accurate to 6 decimal places with only 6-figure numbers.
items.prompt: Why are these particular fractions so good?

options.text: They are 'convergents' of pi's continued fraction expansion, which generates the BEST possible rational approximations — no smaller-denominator fraction can be closer
They are products of pi's digits
All irrationals have such good approximations

items.reveal_title: Continued fractions and best rational approximations
items.reveal:
Pi's continued fraction expansion begins: 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(15 + 1/(1 + 1/(292 + 1/(...))))). The 'convergents' formed by truncating give:
3/1, 22/7, 333/106, 355/113, 103993/33102, ...

Each convergent is the best rational approximation to pi for its denominator size (no fraction with a smaller or equal denominator is closer). This is a theorem of continued fractions.

The large coefficient 292 in pi's expansion is why 355/113 is so good — it means the next convergent, after 355/113, only kicks in at much larger denominators. So 355/113 is unusually accurate for its size.

The golden ratio phi has continued fraction 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + ...)), all 1s — making it the irrational hardest to approximate by rationals. This 'most irrational' property is why phi appears in plant phyllotaxis and quasicrystals.

Diophantine approximation studies exactly how well an irrational can be approximated by rationals. Roth's theorem (1955) gives sharp bounds for algebraic numbers; the field overlaps with number theory at every turn.
items.why: Approximating irrationals feels like it should give roughly similar fractions. Continued fractions give a precise algorithm for the BEST approximations and reveal why some irrationals are 'harder' than others.

items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: Compound interest of 7% turns 100 into 14,974 over 75 years
items.claim: Simple interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 + (75 x 7) = 625. Compound interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 x 1.07^75 = 14,974. The same rate, the same time. Compounding multiplies the result by 24x.
items.prompt: Why does compound interest diverge so dramatically?

options.text: Compound interest grows exponentially (multiplicatively each period); simple interest grows linearly (additively). Over long horizons, exponential growth always vastly exceeds linear, no matter the rate
The two are basically the same after enough time
Compound interest only works for whole-year periods

items.reveal_title: The rule of 72 and the magic of compounding
items.reveal:
Compound interest: each period, interest is paid on (principal + accumulated interest). Mathematically: A = P (1 + r)^n.
Simple interest: A = P (1 + r * n).

Rule of 72: at compound rate r% per year, money doubles in about 72/r years. At 7%, doubling time ~10.3 years. In 75 years that's ~7 doublings, so ~128x the original.

Applied historically: Einstein supposedly called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world' (apocryphal but illustrative). It explains:
- Why starting to save in your 20s vs your 40s makes such a huge difference.
- Why credit card debt at 20% APR explodes if minimum payments are made.
- Why long-run stock returns (averaging ~7% real) translate into vast wealth over careers.

For short horizons (1-2 periods), compound and simple interest are nearly equal. For long horizons, the gap is enormous. The gap is the 'magic' that financial planners try to communicate to young people, often unsuccessfully.

Negative compounding (decay) works the same way: 7% inflation halves purchasing power in ~10 years.
items.why: Linear and exponential are taught as adjacent concepts. They diverge in practice so dramatically that human intuition completely fails for long horizons. Anyone making long-term financial decisions needs to feel this in their bones.
